python-motion-lab.title: Names, values and a small bill
python-motion-lab.idea: A variable gives a name to a value. Keeping quantities separate makes a calculation easier to read and change.
python-motion-lab.code:
price = 12
quantity = 3
total = price * quantity
print(f"Total: {total}")
steps: price and quantity store integers. Their names explain what the numbers mean.
The * operator multiplies; the result is stored in total.
The f-string inserts total inside the displayed text. print ends the line with a newline.
Change quantity to 4 and reason that the output becomes Total: 48 before running it.
python-motion-lab.lesson: A variable is a name for a value, not a promise that the value can never change.

python-motion-lab.title: Convert text before arithmetic
python-motion-lab.idea: User input and file fields often arrive as strings. Convert them when the operation requires numbers.
steps: The quotation marks create text. Adding two strings joins their characters.
int(text) parses an integer from the text; it can raise ValueError for invalid input.
The first print joins "15" and "5". The second adds the numbers 15 and 5.
If text were "fifteen", conversion would fail rather than guess a number.
python-motion-lab.lesson: The same + symbol has different behavior for strings and numbers.

python-motion-lab.title: Filter a list with a loop
python-motion-lab.idea: A loop repeats a small action for each item. An if statement chooses when that action should happen.
steps: Start with an empty result list. Each iteration gives value the next number.
The >= test is true only for 7 and 9.
append adds one accepted item to the end. Input order is preserved.
A list comprehension [v for v in values if v >= 5] expresses the same selection more compactly.
python-motion-lab.lesson: Use the longer loop until the condition and update are clear.

python-motion-lab.title: Write a function with a clear return value
python-motion-lab.idea: A function packages a reusable rule. Returning an answer is different from displaying it.
python-motion-lab.code:
def bill(count, price=10):
    return count * price

first = bill(3)
second = bill(2, price=7)
print(first)
print(second)
steps: def defines a function; its body runs when the function is called.
price=10 supplies a default only when no price argument is provided.
return sends a value back to the caller. Here the caller stores it in a name.
The two print calls display the results; the function itself does not print.
python-motion-lab.lesson: Separate calculation from display so a function can be reused in other contexts.

python-motion-lab.title: Count items with a dictionary
python-motion-lab.idea: A dictionary associates keys with values. It can keep a running count for each label.
steps: The label is the key and its count is the value.
get(label, 0) returns an existing count or zero for a new label.
Adding one and assigning it updates the count for that occurrence.
sorted(counts) sorts keys for predictable display; it does not change the stored counts.
python-motion-lab.lesson: Dictionaries are useful when you need a value associated with each distinct key.

python-motion-lab.title: Understand a list copy
python-motion-lab.idea: Two names can refer to the same mutable list. A shallow copy creates a new outer list, but does not recursively copy nested objects.
python-motion-lab.code:
original = [1, 2]
alias = original
separate = original.copy()
alias.append(3)
print(original)
print(separate)
steps: alias = original does not create a list. Both names point to the same object.
copy creates a new outer list containing the same entries.
Appending through alias therefore changes original, but not separate.
For nested lists, a shallow copy still shares the nested objects; consider the intended ownership before copying.
python-motion-lab.lesson: Assignment and copying are different operations.

python-motion-lab.title: Handle a specific conversion failure
python-motion-lab.idea: An exception lets code report that an operation could not finish normally. Catch the failure you can actually handle.
steps: int succeeds for "3" and "5", adding them to total.
It raises ValueError for "bad". Control moves to the matching except block.
The message records the skipped input rather than silently losing it.
The loop continues, but in some applications rejecting the entire input would be more appropriate.
python-motion-lab.lesson: Choose error handling according to the task instead of catching every exception blindly.

python-motion-lab.title: Generate values one at a time
python-motion-lab.idea: A generator yields a sequence without constructing the entire result list in advance.
steps: Calling squares creates a generator; it does not immediately run every loop iteration.
next requests the first yielded value, 0.
list consumes the remaining values, not the already-consumed first value.
Once exhausted, a generator does not restart; call squares again to create a new one.
python-motion-lab.lesson: A generator is a stateful stream, so consuming it changes what remains.

dsa-motion-lab.title: Linear search: inspect one item at a time
dsa-motion-lab.idea: Linear search works without sorted input. It returns the first matching position, or a clearly specified missing marker.
steps: enumerate supplies the zero-based index and its value.
The first match returns immediately, so the later 3 is not returned.
If the loop ends without a match, -1 is the chosen sentinel.
Worst-case work grows linearly with the list length: O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
dsa-motion-lab.lesson: Document the missing marker so callers do not accidentally use -1 as a valid Python list index.

dsa-motion-lab.title: Binary search: halve a sorted search range
dsa-motion-lab.idea: Binary search needs sorted data. It compares with the middle and discards the half that cannot contain the target.
steps: low and high bound the remaining inclusive range.
Integer division // picks a valid middle index.
The updates exclude the already-compared middle, ensuring progress.
Time is O(log n) on a sorted random-access list; sorting an unsorted input first has its own cost.
dsa-motion-lab.lesson: Never apply this version to an unsorted list and trust the answer.

dsa-motion-lab.title: Use a stack to check brackets
dsa-motion-lab.idea: A stack remembers the most recent unmatched opening bracket. The next closing bracket must match it.
steps: append pushes an opening bracket onto the stack.
pop removes the most recent opener, implementing last-in-first-out order.
A closer with an empty stack or the wrong opener fails immediately.
This checks bracket characters, not a full programming-language grammar; quoted strings are not specially parsed.
dsa-motion-lab.lesson: The stack structure mirrors nested matching. Time and worst-case space are O(n).

dsa-motion-lab.title: Breadth-first search with a queue
dsa-motion-lab.idea: BFS explores an unweighted graph in layers. A queue processes earlier discoveries before later ones.
steps: deque supports removing the oldest queued item efficiently.
Mark nodes seen when they are enqueued, preventing D from being added twice.
Neighbor-list order determines the order among nodes at the same layer.
With adjacency lists, work is O(V+E) for the explored graph; memory tracks the queue and visited nodes.
dsa-motion-lab.lesson: BFS finds shortest edge-count paths in unweighted graphs, not arbitrary weighted shortest paths.

dsa-motion-lab.title: Merge two already-sorted lists
dsa-motion-lab.idea: Keep a pointer into each list. Repeatedly take the smaller next value, then append any remaining tail.
steps: Each pointer identifies the next unused value.
Choosing <= takes an equal value from the left first, preserving cross-list order for ties in a stable merge.
Once either list ends, its partner’s remaining values are already ordered.
Time is O(n+m); the returned list uses O(n+m) space.
dsa-motion-lab.lesson: This merges sorted inputs; it does not sort arbitrary unsorted inputs.

dsa-motion-lab.title: Two-sum with remembered values
dsa-motion-lab.idea: Remember earlier values so that each new value can ask whether its complement has appeared.
steps: For value 7 and target 9, the complement is 2.
Check before inserting the current item, so it cannot pair with itself.
Repeated values can still form a valid pair at different indices.
Expected time is O(n) with ordinary hash-table behavior; extra storage is O(n).
dsa-motion-lab.lesson: Return indices or values deliberately: callers need to know which interpretation they receive.

dsa-motion-lab.title: Dynamic programming: reuse earlier answers
dsa-motion-lab.idea: The number of ways to climb n steps using steps of size 1 or 2 can be built from the two smaller answers.
steps: The final move is either one step from n−1 or two steps from n−2.
The base case n=0 counts one empty sequence; n=1 has one way.
Only the previous two counts are needed, so the code stores two integers.
There are O(n) updates and O(1) stored integer objects; integer bit sizes grow with n.
dsa-motion-lab.lesson: A recurrence plus base cases makes repeated subproblems explicit.

dsa-motion-lab.title: Prefix sums answer range questions quickly
dsa-motion-lab.idea: Precompute totals before each position. A range total is the difference between two prefix totals.
dsa-motion-lab.code:
values = [3, 1, 4, 2]
prefix = [0]
for value in values:
    prefix.append(prefix[-1] + value)

def range_sum(start, stop):
    return prefix[stop] - prefix[start]

print(prefix)
print(range_sum(1, 3))
steps: prefix[k] holds the sum of values before index k.
The query uses a half-open range: start is included and stop is excluded.
For [1,3), subtract prefix[1]=3 from prefix[3]=8 to obtain 1+4=5.
Building costs O(n) time and storage; each valid query costs O(1).
dsa-motion-lab.lesson: If the underlying values change, this stored prefix array must be updated or rebuilt.

unix-motion-lab.title: Print predictable lines with printf
unix-motion-lab.idea: Use a fixed set of fictional names as input. These examples target Bash with GNU/Linux utilities; they do not execute in the web page.
steps: printf is a shell command that formats arguments.
%s means print the next argument as text. The format’s \n means end the line.
The format is reused for each remaining argument, producing one line per name.
Single quotes preserve text literally. This command has a format argument, not a dash-prefixed option.
unix-motion-lab.lesson: Prefer printf for predictable formatting; echo handling of escapes varies across environments.

unix-motion-lab.title: Find matching lines and show their positions
unix-motion-lab.idea: A pipe sends one command’s output to the next command’s input. grep selects lines matching a pattern.
steps: printf supplies three lines to the pipe.
grep reads those lines from standard input.
-n prefixes each match with its original line number, starting at 1.
The pattern ERROR matches these uppercase strings; this example does not use -i for case-insensitive matching.
unix-motion-lab.lesson: Line numbers refer to the input stream. grep normally returns status 1 when no line matches; that is not the same as a tool error.

unix-motion-lab.title: Count repeated labels after sorting
unix-motion-lab.idea: uniq combines adjacent identical lines. Sorting first makes all identical labels adjacent.
unix-motion-lab.code:
export LC_ALL=C
printf '%s\n' 'red' 'blue' 'red' 'blue' 'red' | sort | uniq -c | awk '{print $1, $2}'
steps: LC_ALL=C requests a consistent byte-oriented sorting locale for this example.
sort orders the lines; it does not count them.
uniq -c adds an occurrence count. The -c option means count.
awk prints its first and second whitespace-separated fields with one space, removing uniq’s padding from the displayed output.
unix-motion-lab.lesson: uniq alone only notices adjacent duplicates, so input ordering matters.

unix-motion-lab.title: Sort numbers as numbers
unix-motion-lab.idea: Text sorting and numerical sorting answer different questions. Specify the intended interpretation.
steps: The input lines contain decimal integer text.
sort -n compares numerical values instead of ordinary text order.
Without numerical comparison, text beginning with 1 may come before text beginning with 2.
Add -r together with -n if you deliberately want largest first; this example keeps ascending order.
unix-motion-lab.lesson: GNU sort -n and -g have different numeric parsing rules. Use -g when you specifically need its general numeric format behavior.

unix-motion-lab.title: Filter rows with awk and calculate a total
unix-motion-lab.idea: The fictional input has two whitespace-separated fields: a product name and a quantity.
steps: $2 names the second field. The condition $2 >= 3 selects the first two rows.
Inside braces, total += $2 accumulates selected quantities and print $1 displays the product.
END runs once after all input lines and prints the accumulated total.
The single-quoted program is an awk argument, not a shell variable expression. There are no command flags in this example.
unix-motion-lab.lesson: The field format is part of the example. This is not a general CSV parser with quoted commas or embedded newlines.

unix-motion-lab.title: Replace text using sed
unix-motion-lab.idea: sed can transform a stream without changing any existing file. This example replaces a word on every line.
steps: s introduces substitution; the slashes separate pattern, replacement and modifiers.
red is the pattern and green is the replacement.
The final g replaces every match on each line. Without it, only the first match on each line is replaced.
No -i option is used: the transformed text goes to standard output, not back into a file.
unix-motion-lab.lesson: sed patterns are regular expressions. Special characters need appropriate escaping when you intend literal matching.

unix-motion-lab.title: Select a delimited field with cut
unix-motion-lab.idea: cut extracts positions or fields from simple delimited text.
steps: -d chooses the delimiter, here a colon.
-f 2 selects the second field on each input line.
Single quotes make the colon an explicit literal argument.
The names are omitted and the quantity field is printed on its own line.
unix-motion-lab.lesson: For real CSV with quoting rules, use a CSV-aware parser rather than assuming cut handles every case.

unix-motion-lab.title: Count a filtered result and inspect exit status
unix-motion-lab.idea: Commands communicate through both printed output and an exit status. They are different channels of information.
unix-motion-lab.code:
printf '%s\n' 'INFO ready' 'ERROR disk' 'ERROR network' | grep -c 'ERROR'
printf '%s\n' 'INFO ready' | grep -q 'ERROR'
status=$?
printf 'status=%s\n' "$status"
steps: grep -c prints the number of matching lines, here 2; it counts lines, not occurrences within each line.
grep -q runs quietly and prints no matches.
$? immediately after that pipeline is the status of its last command under this ordinary Bash pipeline configuration. Save it before another command changes it.
Status 1 means no match for grep. The quoted "$status" passes one argument to printf.
unix-motion-lab.lesson: These commands are for an ordinary interactive Bash session without set -e; automatic exit-on-failure scripts need deliberate handling of no-match results.

ml-motion-lab.title: Make a numeric prediction and inspect every contribution
ml-motion-lab.idea: A weighted sum is the same arithmetic as a shopping bill. Each feature contributes its value times its weight.
ml-motion-lab.code:
features = [2, 3]
weights = [4, -1]
contributions = [x * w for x, w in zip(features, weights)]
bias = 1
prediction = sum(contributions) + bias
print(contributions)
print(prediction)
steps: Each feature pairs with its corresponding weight; the assumed list lengths match.
The contributions are 2×4=8 and 3×(−1)=−3.
Their sum is 5, then the fixed bias adds 1.
zip stops at the shorter input, so production code should validate equal lengths rather than silently accept mismatches.
ml-motion-lab.lesson: A negative weight reduces a score; its meaning depends on the feature and fitted model.

ml-motion-lab.title: Measure prediction error with MSE
ml-motion-lab.idea: Mean squared error turns a list of residuals into one nonnegative summary.
ml-motion-lab.code:
actual = [2, 4, 6]
predicted = [1, 5, 6]
errors = [p - y for p, y in zip(predicted, actual)]
squares = [e * e for e in errors]
print(errors)
print(squares)
print(f"MSE={sum(squares) / len(squares):.4f}")
steps: Subtract actual from predicted consistently to define each residual.
Squaring prevents negative and positive residuals from canceling.
Sum the squares and divide by the number of examples.
:.4f displays four decimal places; the internal division is not rounded at that earlier step.
ml-motion-lab.lesson: MSE emphasizes larger errors and uses squared target units. It is not the only sensible loss.

ml-motion-lab.title: Follow gradient descent for three steps
ml-motion-lab.idea: This is a one-parameter training example with a known minimum at w=3.
ml-motion-lab.code:
w = 0.0
rate = 0.1
for step in range(1, 4):
    gradient = 2 * (w - 3)
    w -= rate * gradient
    loss = (w - 3) ** 2
    print(f"step={step} w={w:.4f} loss={loss:.4f}")
steps: The derivative of (w−3)² is 2(w−3), evaluated at the current w.
Subtract rate times gradient to move locally downhill.
Recalculate loss after the update so the printed weight and loss match.
The loss decreases here; a rate that is too large can make this same procedure diverge.
ml-motion-lab.lesson: An optimization example is not evidence that every model will find a global minimum.

ml-motion-lab.title: Calculate softmax without enormous exponentials
ml-motion-lab.idea: Softmax turns scores into positive values summing to one. Subtracting a shared maximum leaves the probabilities unchanged.
ml-motion-lab.code:
from math import exp
scores = [1000.0, 1001.0]
largest = max(scores)
scaled = [exp(x - largest) for x in scores]
total = sum(scaled)
probabilities = [x / total for x in scaled]
print([round(p, 4) for p in probabilities])
print(f"sum={sum(probabilities):.4f}")
steps: Direct exp(1000) can overflow; shifting gives exponent arguments −1 and 0.
Exponentials are positive, then division by their sum normalizes them.
The larger score receives the larger probability.
The example rounds only the displayed list. Very tiny probabilities can still underflow in extreme cases; log-softmax is useful when log probabilities are needed.
ml-motion-lab.lesson: A numerically stable formula can be algebraically equivalent to an unstable one.

ml-motion-lab.title: Compute a Bayes update with counts
ml-motion-lab.idea: Fictional item flags illustrate why a useful detector can still produce many false alarms.
ml-motion-lab.code:
faulty_and_flagged = 8
good_and_flagged = 18
flagged = faulty_and_flagged + good_and_flagged
posterior = faulty_and_flagged / flagged
print(f"Flagged: {flagged}")
print(f"Faulty among flagged: {posterior:.2%}")
steps: Restrict attention to the group already known to be flagged.
Count all flags, including false alarms, to obtain the correct denominator.
Divide the faulty flags by all flags.
:.2% converts a fraction into a displayed percentage with two decimal places.
ml-motion-lab.lesson: This is the probability of a fault given a flag, not the probability of a flag given a fault.

ml-motion-lab.title: Build an attention-weighted mixture
ml-motion-lab.idea: Attention mixes value vectors using weights. This example supplies the weights so the mixing step is easy to inspect.
ml-motion-lab.code:
weights = [0.25, 0.75]
values = [[2, 0], [0, 4]]
result = [
    sum(weight * value[j] for weight, value in zip(weights, values))
    for j in range(2)
]
print(result)
steps: Each value vector has two coordinates.
For the first coordinate, calculate 0.25×2+0.75×0=0.5.
For the second, calculate 0.25×0+0.75×4=3.
A complete attention layer calculates weights from queries and keys; this snippet isolates the weighted-value calculation.
ml-motion-lab.lesson: The vector output keeps its coordinate dimension while combining information across positions.

ml-motion-lab.title: Standardize using training information only
ml-motion-lab.idea: Preprocessing is part of the fitted procedure. Use the training mean and scale for later examples.
ml-motion-lab.code:
from statistics import mean, pstdev
train = [2, 4, 6]
center = mean(train)
scale = pstdev(train)
new_value = 8
z = (new_value - center) / scale
print(f"mean={center:.1f} scale={scale:.4f}")
print(f"new z={z:.4f}")
steps: mean computes the training center. pstdev uses the population denominator over the training values for this scaling convention.
The new value does not enter the fitted mean or scale.
Subtract the stored center and divide by the stored positive scale.
A constant training feature has zero scale and needs an explicit handling rule before division.
ml-motion-lab.lesson: Including held-out data in fitted preprocessing can leak information into evaluation.

ml-motion-lab.title: Check a tiny classifier beyond accuracy
ml-motion-lab.idea: Counts of true and false positives answer different questions from overall accuracy.
ml-motion-lab.code:
tp, fp, fn, tn = 30, 10, 20, 40
precision = tp / (tp + fp)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)
accuracy = (tp + tn) / (tp + fp + fn + tn)
print(f"precision={precision:.2f}")
print(f"recall={recall:.2f}")
print(f"accuracy={accuracy:.2f}")
steps: Precision asks how many predicted positives were actually positive.
Recall asks how many actual positives were found.
Accuracy counts all correct labels over all labels.
The example denominators are nonzero; a reusable implementation needs a documented convention for undefined precision or recall.
ml-motion-lab.lesson: Choose metrics that match the consequences of mistakes, not only the largest-looking score.

statistics-lab.title: Mean, median and two variance conventions
statistics-lab.idea: The standard library can calculate common summaries, but you still need to choose the correct interpretation.
statistics-lab.code:
from statistics import mean, median, pvariance, variance
values = [2, 4, 6, 8]
print(f"mean={mean(values):.1f}")
print(f"median={median(values):.1f}")
print(f"population variance={pvariance(values):.4f}")
print(f"sample variance={variance(values):.4f}")
statistics-lab.output:
mean=5.0
median=5.0
population variance=5.0000
sample variance=6.6667
steps: The mean is 20/4=5. The median averages the middle pair 4 and 6.
Squared distances from 5 are 9,1,1,9; their sum is 20.
pvariance divides by 4, treating this list as the described population.
variance divides by 3 for the usual sample-variance estimator. It requires at least two values.
statistics-lab.lesson: Different denominator conventions answer different questions; neither should be chosen to manipulate a result.

statistics-lab.title: Build a frequency table with percentages
statistics-lab.idea: Count labels first, then divide by the explicitly defined sample size.
statistics-lab.code:
from collections import Counter
answers = ["yes", "no", "yes", "yes", "no"]
counts = Counter(answers)
for label in sorted(counts):
    count = counts[label]
    print(f"{label}: {count} ({count / len(answers):.0%})")
steps: Counter counts each occurrence of each label.
The denominator is all five answers in this example.
Sorting gives a predictable output order for comparison with the expected output.
Missing or multiple-response answers would require an explicit denominator policy.
statistics-lab.lesson: A percentage is meaningful only after its whole has been defined.

statistics-lab.title: Weighted averages for unequal groups
statistics-lab.idea: Combining group averages requires group sizes when the target is the overall observation-level mean.
statistics-lab.code:
group_means = [10, 20]
group_sizes = [2, 8]
total = sum(m * n for m, n in zip(group_means, group_sizes))
combined = total / sum(group_sizes)
print(f"combined mean={combined:.1f}")
print(f"unweighted group mean={sum(group_means) / 2:.1f}")
steps: A group’s mean times its size recovers its total.
Combine totals 20 and 160, then divide by the 10 observations.
The unweighted mean gives each group equal influence, despite different sizes.
Both calculations can have a purpose, but they answer different questions.
statistics-lab.lesson: Weight by observation count only when an individual-level combined mean is the target.

statistics-lab.title: Compute an exact binomial probability
statistics-lab.idea: This calculates one count probability directly for a small independent-trial model.
statistics-lab.code:
from math import comb
n, k, p = 3, 2, 0.5
probability = comb(n, k) * p ** k * (1 - p) ** (n - k)
print(f"arrangements={comb(n, k)}")
print(f"probability={probability:.3f}")
steps: comb(3,2) counts which two trial positions are successes.
p**k is the contribution from successes and (1-p)**(n-k) from failures.
The combination factor includes all three successful arrangements.
The model assumes fixed n, independent trials and the same p in each trial.
statistics-lab.lesson: The formula gives a model probability, not a guarantee about a particular sample.

statistics-lab.title: Show the working in a normal-approximation interval
statistics-lab.idea: This example uses an explicitly supplied standard error and normal critical multiplier. It is not a universal small-sample recipe.
statistics-lab.code:
estimate = 50.0
standard_error = 2.0
critical_value = 1.96
margin = critical_value * standard_error
print(f"margin={margin:.2f}")
print(f"interval=[{estimate - margin:.2f}, {estimate + margin:.2f}]")
steps: A standard error describes uncertainty in the estimate, not spread of individual observations.
Multiply by the critical value to obtain the margin.
Subtract and add the margin to build the interval.
Normal approximation and standard-error validity need justification; a t or design-based method may be appropriate instead.
statistics-lab.lesson: The confidence interpretation belongs to the interval procedure and its assumptions.

statistics-lab.title: Analyze paired changes rather than unrelated groups
statistics-lab.idea: Before and after values must remain matched to the same units.
statistics-lab.code:
from statistics import mean, stdev
from math import sqrt
before = [5, 7, 9, 10]
after = [6, 9, 12, 14]
differences = [b - a for a, b in zip(before, after)]
average = mean(differences)
se = stdev(differences) / sqrt(len(differences))
print(differences)
print(f"mean change={average:.4f}")
print(f"SE={se:.4f}")
print(f"t={average / se:.4f}")
steps: Subtract before from after for each matched unit, yielding the differences.
Calculate the mean and sample SD of differences, not two unrelated outcome SDs.
Divide that SD by √number of pairs to get the SE under the independence assumptions.
The statistic needs an appropriate t reference with 3 degrees of freedom for a p-value; this snippet stops at the statistic.
statistics-lab.lesson: A paired analysis depends on valid matching and appropriate assumptions about the differences.

statistics-lab.title: Fit a small least-squares line
statistics-lab.idea: This hand-written calculation exposes the arithmetic of simple regression without an external package.
statistics-lab.code:
from statistics import mean
x, y = [1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 5]
mx, my = mean(x), mean(y)
numerator = sum((a - mx) * (b - my) for a, b in zip(x, y))
denominator = sum((a - mx) ** 2 for a in x)
slope = numerator / denominator
intercept = my - slope * mx
print(f"slope={slope:.4f}")
print(f"intercept={intercept:.4f}")
print(f"prediction at 4={intercept + slope * 4:.4f}")
steps: Center x and y around their own means.
The slope is their centered cross-product sum divided by the centered x squared sum.
Choose the intercept so the line passes through the two means.
Prediction at 4 is beyond the observed x range 1–3, so it is an extrapolation that needs caution.
statistics-lab.lesson: If every x were equal, the denominator would be zero and this slope would not be identifiable.

statistics-lab.title: Enumerate all bootstrap resamples of a tiny sample
statistics-lab.idea: For three observations there are only 3³=27 ordered same-size bootstrap samples, so exact enumeration is practical as a demonstration.
statistics-lab.code:
from itertools import product
from statistics import mean
values = [2, 4, 6]
bootstrap_means = [mean(sample) for sample in product(values, repeat=3)]
print(f"resamples={len(bootstrap_means)}")
print(f"average of means={mean(bootstrap_means):.1f}")
print(f"range={min(bootstrap_means):.1f} to {max(bootstrap_means):.1f}")
statistics-lab.output:
resamples=27
average of means=4.0
range=2.0 to 6.0
steps: product with repeat=3 lists ordered draws with replacement, including repetitions such as (2,2,6).
Each ordered resample has equal probability under this empirical sampling model.
Compute a mean for every resample to examine a bootstrap distribution.
The full minimum-to-maximum range is not a 95% confidence interval. Enumeration grows exponentially and is only for this tiny example.
statistics-lab.lesson: Resampling reuses observed information; it does not create 27 new independent real-world studies.
